title: Nimble SDK Prefetcher and Fragmented Toolflow PRD Notes
body:
Context and intent:

This is a working PRD-style notes doc for a lightweight SDK pattern ("nimble prefetcher") that optimizes perceived latency and tool-call fidelity for mobile and low-bandwidth clients calling the Redwood Hosted API. It focuses on three intertwined areas: incremental/streaming output, a compact tool-handshake for partial/fragmented toolflows, and an opinionated structured-output surface that keeps client ergonomics simple while enabling server-side fallbacks and telemetry.

Why now / problem statement:
- Product teams building embedded assistants report high variance in cold-start latency for tool calls and poor UX when partial results need tool-backed enrichment (search, DB lookup, function execution).
- Clients with intermittent connectivity (mobile, edge) need a low-footprint SDK ergonomics surface that supports resumable partial responses, speculative prefetching of likely tool results, and a compact way to commit or roll back tool-side changes.
- Existing hosted streaming patterns focus on monolithic frames or heavy handshake protocols that increase roundtrips. We need a nimble option that reduces SDK complexity and network bytes while preserving strong correctness for tool invocation semantics.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce median first-tool-response latency perceived by clients by 25% for mobile scenarios (measured as time to first meaningful token + tool result).
- Lower network bytes for handshake per tool-call by >= 40% compared to the current full-json tool-handshake in baseline experiments.
- Provide structured-output contract that enables automatic fallback to lighter-weight model-only responses when tools are unavailable, with clear provenance headers for audit.
- SDK ergonomics: single small interface (<= 3 calls) for typical streaming + tool scenarios; compatibility with existing hosted streaming API (opt-in).

Non-goals:
- This doc does not propose a full rewrite of the hosted tool graph orchestration (no change to server-side DAG execution semantics).
- Not targeting heavy server-to-server batch workloads — primary focus is client-initiated interactive flows.

User personas and stories:
- Mobile Product Engineer: wants a low-friction integration so the assistant can show partial suggestions while a search tool finishes. "I want the SDK to give me a partial answer quickly and then smoothly insert a tool result when ready without flicker."
- Platform Integrator (internal): needs to debug tool fallbacks and link telemetry back to prompt sets. "I need consistent structured output and provenance so we can detect regressions when model quality drifts." 
- Developer on constrained networks: needs the client to be tolerant of reconnections and to continue a partial session. "If a mobile app loses connection, it should resume the stream and rehydrate tool results without a full restart."

High-level design overview:
- Nimble Prefetcher (client-side heuristic): SDK exposes an optional lightweight prefetch API that can speculatively request a small set of tool candidates at call start. The server runs them in a low-cost precompute path when capacity allows and returns compact indexes to the client in the initial stream.
- Fragmented Toolflow packets: Instead of a single large tool-handshake object, we send an initial minimal tokenized promise (tool id, minimal args hash, confidence weight). The server can respond with incremental fragments when partial tool outputs become available.
- Structured output shards: Responses are encoded as a small sequence of typed shards ("text-frag", "tool-idx", "tool-frag", "prov"), each compactly framed. Clients recompose shards incrementally.
- Commit/abort micro-protocol: Tool operations that have side effects expose an explicit commit token in the stream. The SDK only surfaces the tool result to the host app after commit or exposes a tentative result if the app opts-in.

API surface (SDK):
- startInteraction(prompt, opts): returns sessionId + initial stream reader; opts.prefetchCandidates: [toolId,...], opts.speculative=true/false
- onStream(callback): receives shards immediately as they arrive; callback receives (shardType, payload) where shardType is one of ["text-frag","tool-idx","tool-frag","prov","end"]
- commitToolResult(sessionId, commitToken): informs server client has accepted a side-effecting tool action (optional; default server auto-commit policy applies)

Streaming framing notes (compact):
- Use newline-delimited compact JSON lines for shards to reduce framing overhead vs full enveloping. Each line includes: type, session, seq, payloadBase64 (for tool-frag binary), minimal prov header. This keeps client parsers simple and reduces bytes for short fragments.
- Example shard: {"t":"tool-idx","s":"sid-123","seq":4,"p":"search:3,kg:1"}
- Tool fragments can be binary (attachments) but will usually be small text results; encode as base64 if binary.

Tool handshake semantics (fragmented and nimble):
- Initial tool promise: client can include an ordered list of speculative tool candidates with small arg hashes. Server uses these to pre-warm cached tool outputs (if available) and returns tool-idx fragments early in the stream to hint rank.
- When a tool result is needed, the model will emit an explicit tool-idx shard referencing the candidate; server will stream the tool-frag shards as they arrive.
- If a tool is unavailable, the server emits a tool-fallback shard with a reason code and optionally a model-generated fallback snippet.
- For side-effecting tools, the server includes a provisional token in the tool-frag; the client may call commitToolResult if it wants the side-effect to be considered final. Servers maintain idempotency keys.

Structured output and schema versioning:
- Responses are intentionally lightweight: each shard has a single short type code and a compact payload. We define v1 schema: shard types and payload patterns.
- We include a simple schema version header in the initial stream so SDKs can handle minor changes gracefully.
- Provenance shard ("prov") includes a minimal lineage string: model:ver, tool:ids (optional), confidenceScore, timestamp. Keep this short to avoid bloating the stream.

SDK ergonomics: developer-facing patterns:
- Default integration path: call startInteraction; render text-frag shards immediately; when tool-frag arrives, animate an in-place enrichment (no full re-render). The SDK will provide a small helper to map tool-frag -> anchor token position to make insertion deterministic.
- Two ergonomics modes: "auto-commit" (default) where SDK accepts server commit semantics and surfaces final results; "confirm-first" where SDK shows tentative tool results and requires explicit user acceptance before commitToolResult. Useful for destructive actions.
- Small binary size target: the default JS SDK bundle for this mode should be < 35KB gzipped (code + parser). Mobile SDKs should aim for similarly tiny parsers implemented in native code.

Observability and telemetry (required fields):
- Critical per-session fields emitted as sampling events: sessionId, startTs, firstTextFragTs, firstToolIdxTs, firstToolFragTs, commitTs (if any), fallbackReason (if any), connectivityResumes count, schemaVersion.
- Provide a lightweight trace-id that ties shards to existing request traces in the Console. Keep default telemetry opt-in for user-level PII concerns.

Fallback and graceful degradation:
- If the client indicates low bandwidth (opts.networkHint = "low"), server will suppress prefetch and only include tool-idx hints; full tool-frag will be provided only when the model explicitly requests it.
- When schema mismatch occurs (client older than server v1.x), server includes downgrade hints and emits a compatibility layer with plain text-fallback shards.

Security and safety considerations:
- Tool fragments that include sensitive results must be redacted unless the client session has the correct access token scope. The protocol includes per-shard access scope tags; client SDK validates token scope before rendering sensitive shards.
- Side-effecting tool commits must require idempotency keys and double-confirmation in "confirm-first" mode.

Migration plan / rollout strategy:
- Phase 0 (experiments): Server-side feature-flag + opt-in SDK preview for internal apps and a few partners. Collect telemetry, monitor latencies, byte savings, and UX regressions. Target 4 weeks of telemetry.
- Phase 1 (limited beta): Expose public opt-in header and SDK preview for select customers. Provide migration guide for existing streaming SDKs with a compatibility shim.
- Phase 2 (gradual): Flip default behavior for new low-latency routes after 8 weeks if metrics meet thresholds. Keep old handshake available via explicit schemaVersion param for backward compatability.

Success metrics (ops + product):
- Infrastructure: % of tool-calls handled via nimble prefetch path versus baseline, average per-call bytes, error/fallback rate.
- Product: perceived latency improvement (cohort A/B), conversion to commit for confirm-first flows, crash/reconnect rates on mobile.

Open questions / risks (to resolve):
- Prefetch cost: how do we bill speculative prefetch operations? Model suggests either a tiny flat fee per candidate or absorb into initial tokens; need billing input (finance).
- Consistency model: if speculative prefetch returns an outdated cached tool result, we need clear expiry semantics and a TTL policy tied to the prefetch window.
- SDK complexity vs features: ensure the SDK surface remains <=3 calls; can we implement commit/confirm semantics without expanding APIs?
- Telemetry PII: what fields require automatic masking? Privacy team input required.

Immediate next steps / action items:
- [Priya] Draft a compact shard spec (types + minimal payload schemas) and share with runtime and DRI for security (due 2025-02-25).
- [Ethan] Prototype JS SDK parser for shard lines; measure gzipped size (due 2025-02-28).
- [Marisol] Run internal A/B on mobile app with opt-in flag and capture first-tool-response latency (due 2025-03-07).
- [Liam] Cost model sketch for speculative prefetch and proposed billing approaches; sync with finance (due 2025-03-03).
- [Sofia] Write accessibility and UX guidance for in-place enrichment insertion and commit flows (due 2025-03-05).

Notes / brainstorming fragments (raw):
- consider hedged micro-frames for very slow tools: send a tiny placeholder immediately that reserves a token-space on client UI so insertion doesn't shift layout.
- tiny provenance: compress model ver to short token (m1->rwd-v1).
- experiment: have prefetch candidates linked to prompt anchors so we can cancel prefetches if the model's trajectory diverges early.
- low-bandwidth mode: prefer tool-idx hints + model-synth fallback; allow app to request full tool only on user tap.

Appendix: example mock stream (line-delimited JSON) v1:
{"hdr":"schema:v1","s":"sid-123","ts":"2025-02-18T17:02:03Z"}
{"t":"text-frag","s":"sid-123","seq":1,"p":"Hello, here are options: "}
{"t":"tool-idx","s":"sid-123","seq":2,"p":"search:0,kg:1"}
{"t":"text-frag","s":"sid-123","seq":3,"p":"(1) Quick summary — pulling latest docs..."}
{"t":"tool-frag","s":"sid-123","seq":4,"id":"search:0","p":"SGVsbG8gd29ybGQ="}  // base64 'Hello world'
{"t":"prov","s":"sid-123","seq":5,"p":"m1:4|search:0|0.93"}
{"t":"end","s":"sid-123","seq":6}
